description: ARASYN is a student team joining NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 for the first time. We share a passion for space exploration, science, technology, and creative storytelling. Driven by curiosity and teamwork, we aim to develop meaningful ideas, explore new challenges, and inspire others. We value creativity, research, communication, problem-solving, and a willingness to learn together.
summary:
What if you could walk on the Moon and meet the machines we left there?

Space Museum is a 3D museum that runs in the browser. Visitors board a spaceship cockpit, fly to the Moon or Mars, and step out to walk, run and jump in real lunar or Martian gravity, with Earth hanging in the lunar sky. Five real machines wait for them: Apollo 15’s Falcon, Surveyor 3, the Viking 1 Lander and Orbiter, and the Ingenuity helicopter.

Every machine comes alive. A voiced timeline reshapes its 3D model at each stop. Tap a part to see what it did and how it could be recycled. Ask the machine questions, discover how it still benefits Earth today and how it could help people living there one day, then play a short game built on its real mission. Commander Nova welcomes visitors, leads a guided tour, and gives them a visitor pass and a time capsule.

We built it for school students and for people with disabilities: fully in Arabic and English, with 638 recorded voice lines, a spoken audio guide, on-screen text for every word, one-switch and easy-read modes. Every fact comes from NASA mission data, with its source shown.
details:
What it does and how it works
Space Museum is a 3D museum that runs in any web browser. Visitors start in a spaceship cockpit, fly to the Moon or Mars, land, and walk among five real machines humans left behind: Apollo 15’s lunar module Falcon, Surveyor 3, the Viking 1 Lander and Orbiter, and the Ingenuity helicopter. Movement follows real lunar and Martian gravity, and Earth is visible in the lunar sky.

When a visitor opens a machine, they can:

  • rotate its 3D model,
  • play a voiced timeline (up to 16 stops) that changes the model at each stop,
  • tap a part to highlight it and read what it did and an idea for recycling it,
  • ask the machine questions and see the source of each answer,
  • read how it benefits Earth today and how it could help people living there one day,
  • play a short game based on its real mission.

Commander Nova welcomes visitors at the reception, leads a guided tour, and gives a visitor pass and a time capsule.

Benefits and intended impact
The stories of these machines usually live in long technical pages in English. We wanted school students, and people who are often left out, to experience them. The museum is fully in Arabic and English, with 638 recorded voice lines. Visitors choose how they experience it:

  • blind or low vision: audio guide, spoken descriptions, sound that shows the way;
  • deaf or hard of hearing: every spoken word on screen, a visible direction arrow;
  • limited movement: one-switch mode and assisted games;
  • dyslexia and children: easy-read text and larger text;
  • sensitive to motion: no flashing or shaking.

We plan to measure impact with a short quiz before and after a visit, and by timing how long a blind visitor needs to reach a machine and hear its story.

Tools we used
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file; three.js for the 3D scene, with GLTF/Draco 3D models; the browser’s Web Audio and Speech APIs; ElevenLabs for the recorded voices, generated with a Python script; Playwright for automated testing; GitHub Pages for hosting.

What makes it creative
Visitors do not read about a machine; they walk up to it, hear it tell its story, and play its mission. Each machine is connected to recycling and to life on Earth, so a piece of history becomes a lesson about the future.

Factors we considered
Accuracy: every fact comes from NASA mission data, and ideas about the future are clearly labelled as ideas to imagine. Accessibility: built in from the start, not added later. Performance: the museum lowers its graphics quality automatically on slower computers. Honesty about limits: the 3D library needs an internet connection, and we have not yet tested the museum with blind or deaf users. That testing is our next step.
